title: AI Risk Management: A Practical Governance and Testing Guide
description: A working framework for identifying AI risks, testing failure modes, assigning ownership, and monitoring systems after release.
author: PilotStack Team

sections.title: Inventory the AI system and its purpose
sections.body: Record each AI use case, business owner, vendor, model or service, data sources, users, and actions the system can take. State what the system is allowed to do and what is explicitly out of scope. Risk depends on context: an internal brainstorming assistant has a different impact profile from a tool that influences eligibility, financial decisions, or access to essential services. Do not classify risk from the model name alone; consider the whole workflow and the people affected.

sections.title: Assess impact and likelihood
sections.body: For each use case, identify harms from incorrect output, bias, privacy leakage, prompt injection, misuse, service interruption, and over-reliance. Estimate severity and likelihood using a documented scale, and record the evidence behind the rating. Include downstream effects: a small error repeated at scale can be more serious than an isolated visible failure. Prioritize controls for risks that could materially affect people, security, compliance, or business continuity.

sections.title: Test realistic failure modes
sections.body: Build a test set containing normal requests, ambiguous inputs, adversarial instructions, outdated facts, missing data, and attempts to retrieve restricted information. Measure both successful completion and safe refusal. Have domain experts review cases where the right answer is uncertain. Repeat tests after changes to the model, prompts, retrieval sources, integrations, or permissions. Record severity and reproducibility, not just a single pass/fail score.

sections.title: Protect data and access
sections.body: Minimize the data sent to the system, separate user permissions from model instructions, and apply least privilege to connected tools. Treat retrieved documents and user-provided text as untrusted input. Keep secrets out of prompts, log access appropriately, and verify deletion and retention behavior with the vendor. For retrieval systems, test that access rules are enforced at retrieval time and not merely described in the prompt.

sections.title: Define human oversight and escalation
sections.body: Specify which outputs require review, who can override a result, and what happens when confidence is low or the system is unavailable. Reviewers need the time, context, and authority to reject a recommendation. For high-impact uses, preserve a non-AI fallback and provide a clear route to challenge or correct an outcome. Avoid nominal human approval that simply rubber-stamps the model.

sections.title: Set release gates and accountability
sections.body: Name an accountable owner for each material risk and define release criteria, incident severity levels, response times, and rollback authority. Keep evidence of evaluations, approved configurations, vendor terms, known limitations, and exceptions. Involve legal, privacy, security, accessibility, and domain experts where the use case requires it. A policy is useful only when teams can follow it during ordinary delivery.

sections.title: Monitor, respond, and reassess
sections.body: After release, monitor error reports, output quality, cost, latency, unusual access patterns, and changes in input distribution. Establish a way to pause a risky feature, revert a prompt or model change, notify affected users, and preserve evidence for investigation. Reassess risk when the purpose, data, users, or connected actions change. Governance should be a repeatable operating process, not a one-time checklist.
